<system-reminder>
## Swarm Mode

You are now in "agent swarm" mode. The user may send tasks that require a large number of parallel subagents.

## Workflow

You do not need to use TodoList to record this workflow.

1. First, you may need to do a small amount of exploratory work before deciding how to divide the task across subagents. You may not need subagents during this exploratory phase.

2. After exploring, if you are convinced no subagent is needed to complete the task, tell the user why and wait for further instructions; otherwise, continue with the appropriate delegation.

3. Once you have enough context, do not handle the main work yourself. Use AgentSwarm with a `prompt_template` containing the `{{item}}` placeholder and an `items` array for the requested or appropriate number of subagents, partitioning the problem so each item gives one subagent a distinct part of the work. Pass `subagent_type` when the whole swarm should use a non-default subagent profile.

## Coordination

- Give each subagent a distinct scope of work.
- Avoid duplicating work across subagents.
- Avoid assigning conflicting changes or responsibilities to different subagents.
- Remember that subagents have your full capabilities. Do not overload their prompts with excessive detail; only describe the necessary background and each subagent's specific task.
- Unless the user explicitly specifies a lower limit, do not try to conserve the number of agents. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents and queues launches automatically, so decompose work as finely as possible while keeping subagent responsibilities non-conflicting; combine tasks only when they are genuinely inseparable. If the subagents only need to read, inspect, or report back without making changes, their scopes may overlap slightly.
</system-reminder>

payload.prompt:
You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this - finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool - does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only - your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

199	.B \-x
200	(default) sets the justification according to whether left-to-right or
201	right-to-left text is selected.  Left-to-right text will be flush-left,
202	while right-to-left text will be flush-right.  (Left-to-right versus
203	right-to-left text is controlled by
204	.BR \-L ,
205	.B \-R
206	and
207	.BR \-X .)
208	
209	.TP
210	.B \-t
211	.PD 0
212	.TP
213	.BI \-w \ outputwidth
214	.PD
215	These options control the
216	.IR outputwidth ,
217	or the screen width
218	.B FIGlet
219	assumes when formatting its output.
220	.B FIGlet
221	uses the
222	.I outputwidth
223	to determine when to break lines and how to center
224	the output.  Normally,
225	.B FIGlet
226	assumes 80 columns so that people with wide terminals
227	won't annoy the people they e-mail
228	.B FIGlet
229	output to.
230	.B \-t
231	sets the
232	.I outputwidth
233	to the terminal width.  If the terminal width cannot be determined,
234	the previous
235	.I outputwidth
236	is retained.
237	.B \-w
238	sets the
239	.I outputwidth
240	to the given integer.  An
241	.I outputwidth
242	of 1 is a special value that tells
243	.B FIGlet
244	to print each non-space FIGcharacter, in its entirety, on a separate line,
245	no matter how wide it is.
246	
247	.TP
248	.B \-p
249	.PD 0
250	.TP
251	.B \-n
252	.PD
253	These options control how
254	.B FIGlet
255	handles newlines.
256	.B \-p
257	puts
258	.B FIGlet
259	into ``paragraph mode'', which eliminates some unnecessary line
260	breaks when piping a multi-line file through
261	.BR FIGlet .
262	In paragraph mode,
263	.B FIGlet
264	treats line breaks within a paragraph as if they were merely blanks
265	between words.  (Specifically,
266	.B \-p
267	causes
268	.B FIGlet
269	to convert any newline which is not preceded by a newline and not
270	followed by a space character into a blank.)
271	.B \-n
272	(default) puts
273	.B FIGlet
274	back to normal, in which every newline
275	.B FIGlet
276	reads causes it to produce a line break.
277	
278	.TP
279	.B \-D
280	.PD 0
281	.TP
282	.B \-E
283	.PD
284	.B \-D
285	switches to the German (ISO 646-DE) character set.  Turns `[', `\e'
286	and `]' into umlauted A, O and U, respectively.  `{', `|' and `}' turn
287	into the respective lower case versions of these.  `~' turns into s-z.
288	.B \-E
289	turns off
290	.B \-D
291	processing.
292	These options are deprecated,
293	which means they probably will not appear
294	in the next version of
295	.BR FIGlet .
296	
297	.TP
298	.BI \-C \ controlfile
299	.PD 0
300	.TP
301	.B \-N
302	.PD
303	These options deal with
304	.B FIGlet
305	.IR controlfiles .
306	A 
307	.I controlfile
308	is a file containing a list of commands that
309	.B FIGlet
310	executes each time it reads a character.  These commands can map certain
311	input characters to other characters, similar to the Unix
312	.B tr
313	command or the
314	.B FIGlet
315	.B \-D
316	option.
317	.B FIGlet
318	maintains a list of
319	.IR controlfiles ,
320	which is empty when
321	.B FIGlet
322	starts up.
323	.B \-C
324	adds the given
325	.I controlfile
326	to the list.
327	.B \-N
328	clears the
329	.I controlfile
330	list, cancelling the effect of any previous
331	.BR \-C .
332	.B FIGlet
333	executes the commands in all
334	.I controlfiles
335	in the list.  See
336	the file
337	.IR figfont.txt ,
338	provided with FIGlet,
339	for details on how to write a
340	.IR controlfile .
341	
342	.TP
343	.B \-s
344	.PD 0
345	.TP
346	.B \-S
347	.PD 0
348	.TP
349	.B \-k
350	.PD 0
351	.TP
352	.B \-W
353	.PD
354	.TP
355	.B \-o
356	.PD
357	These options control how
358	.B FIGlet
359	spaces the FIGcharacters that it outputs.
360	.B \-s
361	(default) and
362	.B \-S
363	cause ``smushing''.
364	The FIGcharacters are displayed
365	as close together as possible,
366	and overlapping sub-characters are removed.
367	Exactly which sub-characters count as ``overlapping''
368	depends on the font's
369	.IR layoutmode ,
370	which is defined by the font's author.
371	.B \-k
372	causes ``kerning''.  As many blanks as possible are
373	removed between FIGcharacters, so that they
374	touch, but the FIGcharacters are not smushed.
375	.B \-W
376	makes
377	.B FIGlet
378	display all FIGcharacters at their full width,
379	which may be fixed or variable, depending on the font.
380	
381	The difference between
382	.B \-s
383	and
384	.B \-S
385	is that
386	.B \-s
387	will not smush a font whose author specified
388	kerning or full width as the default
389	.IR layoutmode ,
390	whereas
391	.B \-S
392	will attempt to do so.
393	
394	If there is no information in the font
395	about how to smush,
396	or if the
397	.B \-o
398	option is specified,
399	then the FIGcharacters are ``overlapped''.
400	This means that after kerning,
401	the first subcharacter of
402	each FIGcharacter is removed.
403	(This is not done if a FIGcharacter
404	contains only one subcharacter.)
405	
406	.TP
407	.BI \-m \ layoutmode
408	Specifies an explicit
409	.I layoutmode
410	between
411	.B 1
412	and
413	.BR 63 .
414	.I Smushmodes
415	are explained in
416	.IR figfont.txt ,
417	which also provides complete information
418	on the format of a
419	.B FIGlet
420	font.
421	For the sake of backward compatibility
422	with versions of
423	.B FIGlet
424	before 2.2,
425	.B \-m0
426	is equivalent to
427	.BR \-k ,
428	.B \-m-1
429	is equivalent to
430	.BR \-W ,
431	and
432	.B \-m-2
433	is equivalent to
434	.BR \-s .
435	The
436	.B \-m
437	switch is normally
438	used only by font designers testing the various
439	.I layoutmodes
440	with a new font.
441	
442	.TP
443	.B \-v
444	.PD 0
445	.TP
446	.BI \-I \ infocode
447	.PD
448	These options print various information about
449	.BR FIGlet ,
450	then exit.  If several of these options are given on the command line, only
451	the last is executed, and only after
452	all other command-line options have been dealt with.
453	
454	.B \-v
455	prints version and copyright information, as well as a ``Usage: ...''
456	line.
457	.B \-I
458	prints the information corresponding to the given
459	.I infocode
460	in a consistent, reliable (i.e., guaranteed to be the same in
461	future releases) format.
462	.B \-I
463	is primarily intended to be used by programs that use
464	.BR FIGlet .
465	.I infocode
466	can be any of the following.
467	.RS
468	.TP
469	.BR -1 " Normal operation (default)."
470	This
471	.I infocode
472	indicates that
473	.B FIGlet
474	should operate normally, not giving any informational printout,
475	printing its input in the selected font.
476	.TP
477	.BR 0 " Version and copyright."
478	This is identical to
479	.BR \-v .
480	.TP
481	.BR 1 " Version (integer)."
482	This will print the version of your copy of
483	.B FIGlet
484	as a decimal integer.  The main version number is multiplied by 10000,
485	the sub-version number is multiplied by 100, and the sub-sub-version
486	number is multiplied by 1.  These are added together, and the result is
487	printed out.  For example,
488	.B FIGlet
489	2.2 will print
490	.RB `` 20200 ''
491	, version 2.2.1 will print
492	.RB `` 20201 ''.
493	Similarly, version 3.7.2 would print
494	.RB `` 30702 ''.
495	These numbers are guaranteed to be
496	ascending, with later versions having higher numbers.  Note that
497	the first major release of
498	.BR FIGlet ,
499	version 2.0, did not have the
500	.B \-I
501	option.
502	.TP
503	.BR 2 " Default font directory."
504	This will print the default font directory.  It is affected by the
505	.B \-d
506	option.
507	.TP
508	.BR 3 " Font."
509	This will print the name of the font
510	.B FIGlet
511	would use.  It is affected by
512	the
513	.B \-f
514	option.
515	This is not a filename; the
516	.RB `` .flf ''
517	suffix is not printed.
518	.TP
519	.BR 4 " Output width."
520	This will print the value
521	.B FIGlet
522	would use for
523	.IR outputwidth ,
524	the number of columns wide
525	.B FIGlet
526	assumes the screen is.
527	It is affected by the
528	.B \-w
529	and
530	.B \-t
531	options.
532	.TP
533	.BR 5 " Supported font formats."
534	This will list font formats supported by
535	.B FIGlet .
536	Possible formats are
537	.RB `` flf2 ''
538	for FIGfont Version 2
539	.B .flf
540	files and
541	.RB `` tlf2 ''
542	for TOIlet
543	.B .tlf
544	files.
545	.RE
546	.IP
547	If
548	.I infocode
549	is any other positive value,
550	.B FIGlet
551	will simply exit without printing anything.
552	
553	.TP
554	.B \-L
555	.PD 0
556	.TP
557	.B \-R
558	.PD 0
559	.TP
560	.B \-X
561	.PD
562	These options control whether
563	.B FIGlet
564	prints left-to-right or right-to-left.
565	.B \-L
566	selects left-to-right printing.
567	.B \-R
568	selects right-to-left printing.
569	.B \-X
570	(default) makes
571	.B FIGlet
572	use whichever is specified in the font file.
573	
574	Once the options are read,
575	if there are any remaining words on the command line,
576	they are used instead
577	of standard input as the source of text.
578	This feature
579	allows shell scripts to generate large letters without having to dummy
580	up standard input files.
581	
582	An empty argument, obtained by two sequential quotes,
583	results in a line break.
584	
585	.SH EXAMPLES
586	To use
587	.B FIGlet
588	with its default settings, simply type
589	.RS
590	.nf
591	.ft B
592	
593	example% figlet
594	
595	.ft R
596	.fi
597	.RE
598	and then type whatever you like.
599	
600	To change the font, use the
601	.B \-f
602	option, for example,
603	.RS
604	.nf
605	.ft B
606	
607	example% figlet \-f script
608	
609	.ft R
610	.fi
611	.RE
612	
613	Use the
614	.B \-c
615	option if you would prefer centered output:
616	.RS
617	.nf
618	.ft B
619	
620	example% figlet \-c
621	
622	.ft R
623	.fi
624	.RE
625	
626	We have found that the most common use of
627	.B FIGlet
628	is making up large text to be placed in e-mail messages.  For this
629	reason,
630	.B FIGlet
631	defaults to 80 column output.  If you are using a wider terminal, and
632	would like
633	.B FIGlet
634	to use the full width of your terminal, use the
635	.B \-t
636	option:
637	.RS
638	.nf
639	.ft B
640	
641	example% figlet \-t
642	
643	.ft R
644	.fi
645	.RE
646	
647	If you don't want
648	.B FIGlet
649	to smush FIGcharacters into each other, use the
650	.B \-k
651	option:
652	.RS
653	.nf
654	.ft B
655	
656	example% figlet \-k
657	
658	.ft R
659	.fi
660	.RE
661	
662	If
663	.B figlet
664	gets its input from a file, it is often a good idea to use
665	.BR \-p :
666	.RS
667	.nf
668	.ft B
669	
670	example% figlet \-p < myfile
671	
672	.ft R
673	.fi
674	.RE
675	
676	Of course, the above can be combined:
677	.RS
678	.nf
679	.ft B
680	
681	example% figlet \-ptk \-f shadow < anotherfile
682	example% figlet \-cf slant
683	
684	.ft R
685	.fi
686	.RE
687	
688	Finally, if you want to have
689	.B FIGlet
690	take the input from the command
691	line instead of a file:
692	.RS
693	.nf
694	.ft B
695	
696	example% figlet Hello world
697	
698	.ft R
699	.fi
700	.RE
701	
702	.SS Other Things to Try
703	On many systems nice effects can be obtained from the
704	.B lean
705	font by piping it through
706	.BR tr .
707	Some you might want to try are the following:
708	
709	.RS
710	.nf
711	.ft B
712	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' ' ()'
713	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' './\e\e'
714	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' ' //'
715	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' '/  '
716	.ft R
717	.fi
718	.RE
719	
720	Similar things can be done with the
721	.B block
722	font and many of the other
723	.B FIGlet
724	fonts.
725	
726	.SH COMPRESSED FONTS
727	You can compress the fonts and controlfiles
728	using the
729	.B zip
730	archiving program.
731	Place only one font or controlfile in each archive,
732	and rename the archive file (which will have a name
733	ending in
734	.BR .zip )
735	back to
736	.B .flf
737	or
738	.B .flc
739	as the case may be.
740	If you don't rename the file appropriately,
741	.B FIGlet
742	won't be able to find it.
743	
744	.B FIGlet
745	does not care what the filename within the
746	.B .zip
747	archive is, and will process only the first file.
748	
749	The
750	.B .zip
751	format was chosen because tools to create and manipulate it
752	are widely available for free
753	on many platforms.
754	
755	.SH THE STANDARD FONTS
756	
757	Here are a few notes about some of the fonts provided with
758	.IR FIGlet .
759	You can get many other font from the Web site
760	.br
761	http://www.figlet.org/   This location 
762	should also contain the latest version of
763	.B FIGlet
764	and other related utilities.
765	
766	The font
767	.I standard
768	is the basic
769	.B FIGlet
770	font, used when no other font is specified.
771	(This default can be changed when
772	.B FIGlet
773	is compiled on your system.)
774	The
775	.I controlfiles
776	.IR 8859-2 ,
777	.IR 8859-3 ,
778	.IR 8859-4 ,
779	and
780	.I 8859-9
781	are provided for interpreting those character sets,
782	also known as ISO Latin-2 through Latin-5 respectively.
783	The character set 8859-1 (ISO Latin-1) is
784	.B FIGlet's
785	default and requires no special
786	.IR controlfile .
787	
788	Closely related are the fonts
789	.IR slant ,
790	.IR shadow ,
791	.IR small ,
792	.I smslant
793	(both small and slanted),
794	.IR smshadow ,
795	(both small and shadowed),
796	and
797	.IR big .
798	These fonts support only Latin-1, except that
799	.I big
800	supports Greek FIGcharacters as well;
801	the
802	.I controlfiles
803	.I frango
804	(for Greek text written in Latin characters, so-called
805	.RI `` frangovlakhika ''),
806	and
807	.I 8859-7
808	(for mixed Latin/Greek text)
809	are provided.
810	
811	The
812	.I ivrit
813	font is a right-to-left font
814	including both Latin and Hebrew FIGcharacters;
815	the Latin characters are those of the
816	.I standard
817	font.
818	The available
819	.I controlfiles
820	are
821	.IR ilhebrew ,
822	which maps the letters you get
823	by typing on a U.S. keyboard
824	as if it were a Hebrew keyboard;
825	.IR ushebrew ,
826	which makes a reasonable mapping from
827	Latin letters to Hebrew ones;
828	and
829	.IR 8859-8 ,
830	which supports mixed Latin/Hebrew text.
831	.B Warning:
832	.B FIGlet
833	doesn't support bidirectional text,
834	so everything will come out right-to-left,
835	even Latin letters.
836	
837	The fonts
838	.IR terminal ,
839	.IR digital ,
840	and
841	.I bubble
842	output the input character with some decoration around it
843	(or no decoration,
844	in the case of
845	.IR terminal ).
846	The characters coded 128 to 159,
847	which have varying interpretations, are output as-is.
848	You can use the appropriate
849	.I controlfiles
850	to process Latin-2, Latin-3, or Latin-4 (but not Latin-5) text,
851	provided your output device
852	has screen or printer fonts that
853	are appropriate for these character sets.
854	
855	Two script fonts are available:
856	.IR script ,
857	which is larger than
858	.IR standard ,
859	and
860	.IR smscript ,
861	which is smaller.
862	
863	The font 
864	.I lean
865	is made up solely of `/' and `_' sub-characters;
866	.I block
867	is a straight (non-leaning) version of it.
868	
869	The font
870	.I mini
871	is very small, and especially suitable for e-mail signatures.
872	
873	The font
874	.I banner
875	looks like the output of the
876	.B banner
877	program;
878	it is a capitals and small capitals font
879	that doesn't support the ISO Latin-1 extensions
880	to plain ASCII.
881	It does, however, support the Japanese
882	.I katakana
883	syllabary;
884	the
885	.I controlfile
886	.I uskata
887	maps the upper-case and lower-case Latin letters
888	into the 48 basic
889	.I katakana
890	characters,
891	and the
892	.I controlfile
893	.I jis0201
894	handles JIS 0201X (JIS-Roman)
895	mixed Latin and
896	.I katakana
897	text.
898	Furthermore, the
899	.I banner
900	font also supports Cyrillic (Russian)
901	FIGcharacters; the
902	.I controlfile
903	.I 8859-5
904	supports mixed Latin and Cyrillic text,
905	the
906	.I controlfile
907	.I koi8r
908	supports the popular KOI8-R mapping of mixed text,
909	and the
910	.I controlfile
911	.I moscow
912	supports a
913	sensible mapping from Latin to Cyrillic,
914	compatible with the
915	.I moscow
916	font (not supplied).
917	
918	The fonts
919	.I mnemonic
920	and
921	.I safemnem
922	support the mnemonic character set
923	documented in RFC 1345.
924	They implement a large subset of Unicode
925	(over 1800 characters) very crudely,
926	using ASCII-based mnemonic sequences,
927	and are good for getting a quick look
928	at UTF-8 unicode files,
929	using the controlfile
930	.IR utf8 .
931	
932	.SH ENVIRONMENT
933	.TP
934	.B FIGLET_FONTDIR
935	If
936	.RB $ FIGLET_FONTDIR
937	is set, its value is used as a path to search for font files.
938	
939	.SH FILES
940	.PD 0
941	.TP 20
942	.IB file .flf
943	.B FIGlet
944	font file
945	.TP 20
946	.IB file .flc
947	.B FIGlet
948	control file
949	.PD
950	
951	.SH DIAGNOSTICS
952	.B FIGlet's
953	diagnostics are intended to be self-explanatory.  Possible
954	messages are
955	
956	.RS
957	.nf
958	.ft B
959	Usage: ...
960	Out of memory
961	Unable to open font file
962	Not a FIGlet 2 font file
963	Unable to open control file
964	Not a FIGlet 2 control file
965	"\-t" is disabled, since ioctl is not fully implemented.
966	.ft R
967	.fi
968	.RE
969	
970	This last message is printed when the
971	.B \-t
972	option is given, but the operating system in use does not include
973	the system call
974	.B FIGlet
975	uses to determine the terminal width.
976	
977	.B FIGlet
978	also prints an explanatory message if the
979	.B \-F
980	option is given on the command line.
981	The earlier version of
982	.BR FIGlet ,
983	version 2.0, listed the available fonts when the
984	.B \-F
985	option was given.  This option has been removed from
986	.B FIGlet
987	2.1.  It has been replaced by the
988	.B figlist
989	script, which is part of the standard
990	.B FIGlet
991	package.
992	
993	.SH ORIGIN
994	.RB `` FIGlet ''
995	stands for ``Frank, Ian and Glenn's LETters''.  Inspired by Frank's .sig,
996	Glenn wrote (most of) it, and Ian helped.
997

999	.B FIGlet
1000	fonts were inspired by signatures on various UseNet

args.prompt_template:
You are part of a clean-room reverse-engineering effort. /workspace/executable is a compiled FIGlet 2.2.5-like program ("figlet"). We must reimplement it from scratch based ONLY on observed behavior.

HARD RULES:
- Do NOT decompile, disassemble, objdump, strace, ltrace, or read the binary's bytes. Only RUN it with inputs and observe stdout/stderr/exit codes.
- Do NOT use the internet or any package manager to obtain figlet source or docs.
- You MAY read the bundled docs (/workspace/README, /workspace/FAQ, /workspace/figlet.6 man page) and the font/control files in /workspace/fonts and /workspace/assets.
- Create any scratch test files (custom fonts, control files, inputs) under /tmp/yourwork/ (mkdir -p first), NOT in /workspace except your notes file.
- Note: the binary's default font dir /usr/local/share/figlet does not exist, so always pass `-d /workspace/fonts` or `-f <path>` (relative paths resolved against font dir first, then cwd) unless you are specifically testing resolution behavior.

Method: design many small experiments, run the binary, record exact outputs (use `| od -c` or `| cat -A` when whitespace matters; capture stderr separately; record exit codes via `echo $?`).

Deliverable: write a thorough, precise findings document to /workspace/notes/{{item}}.md including exact observed strings (in backticks or code blocks), exact exit codes, and the deduced rules/algorithms. Be exhaustive and precise — someone will implement a clone from your notes without access to you. Also return a 10-line summary of the most important findings.

YOUR ASSIGNED AREA: {{item}}
items: 01-cli: Command-line parsing and informational behavior. Exact 'Usage:' text and where it goes (stdout/stderr) and exit codes for: no args with empty stdin, unknown option (e.g. -z), missing argument for -f/-d/-w/-m/-C/-I, invalid numbers for -w/-m/-I (non-numeric, huge, negative), -- handling, lone '-', option bundling like -ptk, options after message words, multiple messages words (how are they joined? spaces?), empty-string argument behavior (man says line break), -v and -I codes -1..6 and out-of-range positive/negative values, 'only the last -I/-v executed' semantics, -I2 affected by -d order, -I3 affected by -f, -I4 affected by -w/-t, whether usage prints basename of argv[0] or full path (test via bash exec -a or a symlink in /tmp), -F option message, FIGLET_FONTDIR env var behavior (set/unset, with/without -d, colon-separated paths?).

02-fontfile: FIGfont .flf loading semantics. Read /workspace/fonts/standard.flf and a few others (banner, mini, lean, term, big, ivrit) to understand the format empirically. Then craft minimal custom .flf files in /tmp to probe: header fields (signature flf2a, hardblank char, height, baseline, max_length, old_layout, comment_lines, print_direction, full_layout, codetag_count — which are required vs optional, defaults when absent), endmark rules (last char of each row, double endmark on last row), what happens with missing glyphs (e.g. only some of chars 32-126 present), the German 7 chars order after ASCII (196 214 220 228 246 252 223), code-tagged characters (e.g. '0x0391' tagged char, negative tags, decimal tags), blank/short rows, CRLF line endings, comments containing anything, error messages+exit codes for: nonexistent font, empty file, bad signature, truncated file, missing endmarks. How does -f resolve files: with/without .flf suffix, absolute path, path relative to cwd vs fontdir, subdirectory names. What happens when a glyph row is longer than max_length or height mismatches.

03-layout: The layout/rendering engine: kerning, smushing, overlap. Craft tiny custom fonts (2-4 chars, small height, controlled old_layout/full_layout header fields) in /tmp and probe exhaustively: how smush amount is computed (max overlap between right edge of accumulated line and left edge of next char), kerning (-k) vs full width (-W) vs smushing (-s/-S), universal smushing vs the 6 rules (equal char, underscore, hierarchy, opposite pair, big X, hardblank) — determine each rule's exact truth table including which chars smush with which and result precedence, how old_layout values (-1, 0, 1..63) and full_layout interact with -s/-S/-k/-W/-o/-m, horizontal justification (-c/-l/-r/-x) including exact rounding of center padding and interaction with output width, -w values incl. 1 (special), 2, negative, huge; word wrap: when lines break, how whitespace in output rows is trimmed, whether trailing spaces are stripped, exact newline placement at end of output, blank line handling, paragraph mode -p exact semantics, right-to-left (-R) rendering incl. smush side, how chars wider than remaining width are split mid-glyph, what happens when a single glyph exceeds output width.

04-controlfiles: Control file (.flc) semantics. Read the .flc files in /workspace/fonts (646-de, 8859-2, utf8, upper, uskata, hz, frango, moscow, etc.) to learn the format empirically. Probe with crafted .flc files: header (flc2a?), comment handling, mapping commands (single char, ranges like 'a-z A-Z', multiple mappings per line, source/dest columns, multi-char sources?), the 'freeze' command (f) semantics, how many files can be stacked with -C, -N clearing, order of application of stacked controlfiles, error messages+exit codes for missing/malformed controlfiles, whether mapping applies to message args as well as stdin, interaction with -D/-E German mapping (order: controlfiles before/after -D?), mapping of chars to codes >127 and code-tagged glyphs, mapping to multi-byte sequences, what 't' commands or other command letters do (test unknown commands — error or ignored?).

05-tlf-zip: TOIlet .tlf fonts and compressed fonts. Probe using /workspace/assets/emboss.tlf and emboss_1.tlf (run with -f /workspace/assets/emboss or copy to /tmp): how tlf differs from flf in rendering (hardblank char? multibyte glyph chars? charset), whether -I5 lists tlf2 (it printed 'flf2 tlf2'), error when feeding a .tlf as .flf or vice versa, full_layout handling for tlf. Then compressed fonts: create a zip archive containing a single .flf renamed to end in .flf (use `zip` if available, else python3 zipfile) and test whether the binary can read it; test gzip'd fonts (should fail?); note exact behaviors/errors. Also test: does the binary fall back to looking for fontfile.flf.zip? What about a zip with multiple entries or directories? Determine whether it uses an external unzip command (test with PATH stripped via env -i and a restricted PATH).

06-charset-input: Input charset and stream handling. Probe: how input bytes are decoded — plain bytes vs UTF-8 (feed 'é' as latin-1 byte 0xE9 and as UTF-8 0xC3 0xA9, feed Greek/CJK UTF-8, invalid UTF-8 sequences, overlong encodings), which codepoints map to glyphs (fonts have German chars at 196/214/220/228/246/252/223 and code-tagged ones), what happens for chars with no glyph (dropped? printed as-is? blank?), control chars 0-31 (tab expansion? newline handling, CR, NUL), bytes 127-159, high bytes without controlfile. Behavior of -D German mapping exactly ([ \ ] { | } ~ → which codes). Reading from stdin vs message args: line-by-line processing, very long lines (buffer limits? test 10KB+ single line), final line without trailing newline, multiple blank lines, CRLF input, -- end of options. Also test output when input contains only spaces/newlines.

FIGlet - Frank, Ian & Glenn's Letters
======================================

FIGlet is a program that creates large characters out of ordinary screen characters.

Example:

 _ _ _          _   _     _       
| (_) | _____  | |_| |__ (_)___   
| | | |/ / _ \ | __| '_ \| / __|  
| | |   <  __/ | |_| | | | \__ \_ 
|_|_|_|\_\___|  \__|_| |_|_|___(_)

FIGlet can create characters in many different styles and can kern and "smush" 
these characters together in various ways. FIGlet output is generally reminiscent 
of the sort of "signatures" many people like to put at the end of e-mail and 
UseNet messages.

Official FIGlet web page: http://www.figlet.org/
Contact: info@figlet.org


Usage
-----

Basic usage:
    figlet [options] [message]

If no message is provided, FIGlet reads from standard input.

Examples:
    figlet Hello, world!
    echo "Hello, world!" | figlet
    figlet -f banner "Hello"


Command Line Options
--------------------

Font and Layout:
    -f <fontfile>       Use the specified font
    -d <fontdir>        Specify directory for fonts
    -c                  Center the output
    -l                  Left-align the output (default)
    -r                  Right-align the output
    -k                  Use kerning (reduce spacing between characters)
    -W                  Full-width mode (no character smushing)
    -o                  Overlap mode
    -m <mode>           Specify layout mode

357	These options control how
358	.B FIGlet
359	spaces the FIGcharacters that it outputs.
360	.B \-s
361	(default) and
362	.B \-S
363	cause ``smushing''.
364	The FIGcharacters are displayed
365	as close together as possible,
366	and overlapping sub-characters are removed.
367	Exactly which sub-characters count as ``overlapping''
368	depends on the font's
369	.IR layoutmode ,
370	which is defined by the font's author.
371	.B \-k
372	causes ``kerning''.  As many blanks as possible are
373	removed between FIGcharacters, so that they
374	touch, but the FIGcharacters are not smushed.
375	.B \-W
376	makes
377	.B FIGlet
378	display all FIGcharacters at their full width,
379	which may be fixed or variable, depending on the font.
380	
381	The difference between
382	.B \-s
383	and
384	.B \-S
385	is that
386	.B \-s
387	will not smush a font whose author specified
388	kerning or full width as the default
389	.IR layoutmode ,
390	whereas
391	.B \-S
392	will attempt to do so.
393	
394	If there is no information in the font
395	about how to smush,
396	or if the
397	.B \-o
398	option is specified,
399	then the FIGcharacters are ``overlapped''.
400	This means that after kerning,
401	the first subcharacter of
402	each FIGcharacter is removed.
403	(This is not done if a FIGcharacter
404	contains only one subcharacter.)
405	
406	.TP
407	.BI \-m \ layoutmode
408	Specifies an explicit
409	.I layoutmode
410	between
411	.B 1
412	and
413	.BR 63 .
414	.I Smushmodes
415	are explained in
416	.IR figfont.txt ,
417	which also provides complete information
418	on the format of a
419	.B FIGlet
420	font.
421	For the sake of backward compatibility
422	with versions of
423	.B FIGlet
424	before 2.2,
425	.B \-m0
426	is equivalent to
427	.BR \-k ,
428	.B \-m-1
429	is equivalent to
430	.BR \-W ,
431	and
432	.B \-m-2
433	is equivalent to
434	.BR \-s .
435	The
436	.B \-m
437	switch is normally
438	used only by font designers testing the various
439	.I layoutmodes
440	with a new font.
441	
442	.TP
443	.B \-v
444	.PD 0
445	.TP
446	.BI \-I \ infocode
447	.PD
448	These options print various information about
449	.BR FIGlet ,
450	then exit.  If several of these options are given on the command line, only
451	the last is executed, and only after
452	all other command-line options have been dealt with.
453	
454	.B \-v
455	prints version and copyright information, as well as a ``Usage: ...''
456	line.
457	.B \-I
458	prints the information corresponding to the given
459	.I infocode
460	in a consistent, reliable (i.e., guaranteed to be the same in
461	future releases) format.
462	.B \-I
463	is primarily intended to be used by programs that use
464	.BR FIGlet .
465	.I infocode
466	can be any of the following.
467	.RS
468	.TP
469	.BR -1 " Normal operation (default)."
470	This
471	.I infocode
472	indicates that
473	.B FIGlet
474	should operate normally, not giving any informational printout,
475	printing its input in the selected font.
476	.TP
477	.BR 0 " Version and copyright."
478	This is identical to
479	.BR \-v .
480	.TP
481	.BR 1 " Version (integer)."
482	This will print the version of your copy of
483	.B FIGlet
484	as a decimal integer.  The main version number is multiplied by 10000,
485	the sub-version number is multiplied by 100, and the sub-sub-version
486	number is multiplied by 1.  These are added together, and the result is
487	printed out.  For example,
488	.B FIGlet
489	2.2 will print
490	.RB `` 20200 ''
491	, version 2.2.1 will print
492	.RB `` 20201 ''.
493	Similarly, version 3.7.2 would print
494	.RB `` 30702 ''.
495	These numbers are guaranteed to be
496	ascending, with later versions having higher numbers.  Note that
497	the first major release of
498	.BR FIGlet ,
499	version 2.0, did not have the
500	.B \-I
501	option.
502	.TP
503	.BR 2 " Default font directory."
504	This will print the default font directory.  It is affected by the
505	.B \-d
506	option.
507	.TP
508	.BR 3 " Font."
509	This will print the name of the font
510	.B FIGlet
511	would use.  It is affected by
512	the
513	.B \-f
514	option.
515	This is not a filename; the
516	.RB `` .flf ''
517	suffix is not printed.
518	.TP
519	.BR 4 " Output width."
520	This will print the value
521	.B FIGlet
522	would use for
523	.IR outputwidth ,
524	the number of columns wide
525	.B FIGlet
526	assumes the screen is.
527	It is affected by the
528	.B \-w
529	and
530	.B \-t
531	options.
532	.TP
533	.BR 5 " Supported font formats."
534	This will list font formats supported by
535	.B FIGlet .
536	Possible formats are
537	.RB `` flf2 ''
538	for FIGfont Version 2
539	.B .flf
540	files and
541	.RB `` tlf2 ''
542	for TOIlet
543	.B .tlf
544	files.
545	.RE
546	.IP
547	If
548	.I infocode
549	is any other positive value,
550	.B FIGlet
551	will simply exit without printing anything.
552	
553	.TP
554	.B \-L
555	.PD 0
556	.TP
557	.B \-R
558	.PD 0
559	.TP
560	.B \-X
561	.PD
562	These options control whether
563	.B FIGlet
564	prints left-to-right or right-to-left.
565	.B \-L
566	selects left-to-right printing.
567	.B \-R
568	selects right-to-left printing.
569	.B \-X
570	(default) makes
571	.B FIGlet
572	use whichever is specified in the font file.
573	
574	Once the options are read,
575	if there are any remaining words on the command line,
576	they are used instead
577	of standard input as the source of text.
578	This feature
579	allows shell scripts to generate large letters without having to dummy
580	up standard input files.
581	
582	An empty argument, obtained by two sequential quotes,
583	results in a line break.
584	
585	.SH EXAMPLES
586	To use
587	.B FIGlet
588	with its default settings, simply type
589	.RS
590	.nf
591	.ft B
592	
593	example% figlet
594	
595	.ft R
596	.fi
597	.RE
598	and then type whatever you like.
599	
600	To change the font, use the
601	.B \-f
602	option, for example,
603	.RS
604	.nf
605	.ft B
606	
607	example% figlet \-f script
608	
609	.ft R
610	.fi
611	.RE
612	
613	Use the
614	.B \-c
615	option if you would prefer centered output:
616	.RS
617	.nf
618	.ft B
619	
620	example% figlet \-c
621	
622	.ft R
623	.fi
624	.RE
625	
626	We have found that the most common use of
627	.B FIGlet
628	is making up large text to be placed in e-mail messages.  For this
629	reason,
630	.B FIGlet
631	defaults to 80 column output.  If you are using a wider terminal, and
632	would like
633	.B FIGlet
634	to use the full width of your terminal, use the
635	.B \-t
636	option:
637	.RS
638	.nf
639	.ft B
640	
641	example% figlet \-t
642	
643	.ft R
644	.fi
645	.RE
646	
647	If you don't want
648	.B FIGlet
649	to smush FIGcharacters into each other, use the
650	.B \-k
651	option:
652	.RS
653	.nf
654	.ft B
655	
656	example% figlet \-k
657	
658	.ft R
659	.fi
660	.RE
661	
662	If
663	.B figlet
664	gets its input from a file, it is often a good idea to use
665	.BR \-p :
666	.RS
667	.nf
668	.ft B
669	
670	example% figlet \-p < myfile
671	
672	.ft R
673	.fi
674	.RE
675	
676	Of course, the above can be combined:
677	.RS
678	.nf
679	.ft B
680	
681	example% figlet \-ptk \-f shadow < anotherfile
682	example% figlet \-cf slant
683	
684	.ft R
685	.fi
686	.RE
687	
688	Finally, if you want to have
689	.B FIGlet
690	take the input from the command
691	line instead of a file:
692	.RS
693	.nf
694	.ft B
695	
696	example% figlet Hello world
697	
698	.ft R
699	.fi
700	.RE
701	
702	.SS Other Things to Try
703	On many systems nice effects can be obtained from the
704	.B lean
705	font by piping it through
706	.BR tr .
707	Some you might want to try are the following:
708	
709	.RS
710	.nf
711	.ft B
712	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' ' ()'
713	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' './\e\e'
714	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' ' //'
715	example% figlet \-f lean | tr ' _/' '/  '
716	.ft R
717	.fi
718	.RE
719	
720	Similar things can be done with the
721	.B block
722	font and many of the other
723	.B FIGlet
724	fonts.
725	
726	.SH COMPRESSED FONTS
727	You can compress the fonts and controlfiles
728	using the
729	.B zip
730	archiving program.
731	Place only one font or controlfile in each archive,
732	and rename the archive file (which will have a name
733	ending in
734	.BR .zip )
735	back to
736	.B .flf
737	or
738	.B .flc
739	as the case may be.
740	If you don't rename the file appropriately,
741	.B FIGlet
742	won't be able to find it.
743	
744	.B FIGlet
745	does not care what the filename within the
746	.B .zip
747	archive is, and will process only the first file.
748	
749	The
750	.B .zip
751	format was chosen because tools to create and manipulate it
752	are widely available for free
753	on many platforms.
754	
755	.SH THE STANDARD FONTS
756	
757	Here are a few notes about some of the fonts provided with
758	.IR FIGlet .
759	You can get many other font from the Web site
760	.br
761	http://www.figlet.org/   This location 
762	should also contain the latest version of
763	.B FIGlet
764	and other related utilities.
765	
766	The font
767	.I standard
768	is the basic
769	.B FIGlet
770	font, used when no other font is specified.
771	(This default can be changed when
772	.B FIGlet
773	is compiled on your system.)
774	The
775	.I controlfiles
776	.IR 8859-2 ,
777	.IR 8859-3 ,
778	.IR 8859-4 ,
779	and
780	.I 8859-9
781	are provided for interpreting those character sets,
782	also known as ISO Latin-2 through Latin-5 respectively.
783	The character set 8859-1 (ISO Latin-1) is
784	.B FIGlet's
785	default and requires no special
786	.IR controlfile .
787	
788	Closely related are the fonts
789	.IR slant ,
790	.IR shadow ,
791	.IR small ,
792	.I smslant
793	(both small and slanted),
794	.IR smshadow ,
795	(both small and shadowed),
796	and
797	.IR big .
798	These fonts support only Latin-1, except that
799	.I big
800	supports Greek FIGcharacters as well;
801	the
802	.I controlfiles
803	.I frango
804	(for Greek text written in Latin characters, so-called
805	.RI `` frangovlakhika ''),
806	and
807	.I 8859-7
808	(for mixed Latin/Greek text)
809	are provided.
810	
811	The
812	.I ivrit
813	font is a right-to-left font
814	including both Latin and Hebrew FIGcharacters;
815	the Latin characters are those of the
816	.I standard
817	font.
818	The available
819	.I controlfiles
820	are
821	.IR ilhebrew ,
822	which maps the letters you get
823	by typing on a U.S. keyboard
824	as if it were a Hebrew keyboard;
825	.IR ushebrew ,
826	which makes a reasonable mapping from
827	Latin letters to Hebrew ones;
828	and
829	.IR 8859-8 ,
830	which supports mixed Latin/Hebrew text.
831	.B Warning:
832	.B FIGlet
833	doesn't support bidirectional text,
834	so everything will come out right-to-left,
835	even Latin letters.
836	
837	The fonts
838	.IR terminal ,
839	.IR digital ,
840	and
841	.I bubble
842	output the input character with some decoration around it
843	(or no decoration,
844	in the case of
845	.IR terminal ).
846	The characters coded 128 to 159,
847	which have varying interpretations, are output as-is.
848	You can use the appropriate
849	.I controlfiles
850	to process Latin-2, Latin-3, or Latin-4 (but not Latin-5) text,
851	provided your output device
852	has screen or printer fonts that
853	are appropriate for these character sets.
854	
855	Two script fonts are available:
856	.IR script ,
857	which is larger than
858	.IR standard ,
859	and
860	.IR smscript ,
861	which is smaller.
862	
863	The font 
864	.I lean
865	is made up solely of `/' and `_' sub-characters;
866	.I block
867	is a straight (non-leaning) version of it.
868	
869	The font
870	.I mini
871	is very small, and especially suitable for e-mail signatures.
872	
873	The font
874	.I banner
875	looks like the output of the
876	.B banner
877	program;
878	it is a capitals and small capitals font
879	that doesn't support the ISO Latin-1 extensions
880	to plain ASCII.
881	It does, however, support the Japanese
882	.I katakana
883	syllabary;
884	the
885	.I controlfile
886	.I uskata
887	maps the upper-case and lower-case Latin letters
888	into the 48 basic
889	.I katakana
890	characters,
891	and the
892	.I controlfile
893	.I jis0201
894	handles JIS 0201X (JIS-Roman)
895	mixed Latin and
896	.I katakana
897	text.
898	Furthermore, the
899	.I banner
900	font also supports Cyrillic (Russian)
901	FIGcharacters; the
902	.I controlfile
903	.I 8859-5
904	supports mixed Latin and Cyrillic text,
905	the
906	.I controlfile
907	.I koi8r
908	supports the popular KOI8-R mapping of mixed text,
909	and the
910	.I controlfile
911	.I moscow
912	supports a
913	sensible mapping from Latin to Cyrillic,
914	compatible with the
915	.I moscow
916	font (not supplied).
917	
918	The fonts
919	.I mnemonic
920	and
921	.I safemnem
922	support the mnemonic character set
923	documented in RFC 1345.
924	They implement a large subset of Unicode
925	(over 1800 characters) very crudely,
926	using ASCII-based mnemonic sequences,
927	and are good for getting a quick look
928	at UTF-8 unicode files,
929	using the controlfile
930	.IR utf8 .
931	
932	.SH ENVIRONMENT
933	.TP
934	.B FIGLET_FONTDIR
935	If
936	.RB $ FIGLET_FONTDIR
937	is set, its value is used as a path to search for font files.
938	
939	.SH FILES
940	.PD 0
941	.TP 20
942	.IB file .flf
943	.B FIGlet
944	font file
945	.TP 20
946	.IB file .flc
947	.B FIGlet
948	control file
949	.PD
950	
951	.SH DIAGNOSTICS
952	.B FIGlet's
953	diagnostics are intended to be self-explanatory.  Possible
954	messages are
955	
956	.RS
957	.nf
958	.ft B
959	Usage: ...
960	Out of memory
961	Unable to open font file
962	Not a FIGlet 2 font file
963	Unable to open control file
964	Not a FIGlet 2 control file
965	"\-t" is disabled, since ioctl is not fully implemented.
966	.ft R
967	.fi
968	.RE
969	
970	This last message is printed when the
971	.B \-t
972	option is given, but the operating system in use does not include
973	the system call
974	.B FIGlet
975	uses to determine the terminal width.
976	
977	.B FIGlet
978	also prints an explanatory message if the
979	.B \-F
980	option is given on the command line.
981	The earlier version of
982	.BR FIGlet ,
983	version 2.0, listed the available fonts when the
984	.B \-F
985	option was given.  This option has been removed from
986	.B FIGlet
987	2.1.  It has been replaced by the
988	.B figlist
989	script, which is part of the standard
990	.B FIGlet
991	package.
992	
993	.SH ORIGIN
994	.RB `` FIGlet ''
995	stands for ``Frank, Ian and Glenn's LETters''.  Inspired by Frank's .sig,
996	Glenn wrote (most of) it, and Ian helped.
997	
998	Most of the standard
999	.B FIGlet
1000	fonts were inspired by signatures on various UseNet

Available Fonts
---------------

FIGlet comes with numerous fonts stored in the fonts/ directory.
Font files have the extension .flf (FIGlet font) or .flc (FIGlet control file).

Standard fonts include:
    - banner      - Big banner-style letters
    - big         - Large letters
    - block       - Solid block letters  
    - bubble      - Bubble-style letters
    - digital     - Digital display style
    - ivrit       - Hebrew (right-to-left)
    - lean        - Lean letters
    - mini        - Tiny letters
    - script      - Script style
    - shadow      - Letters with shadow
    - slant       - Slanted letters
    - small       - Small letters
    - standard    - Standard font (default)
    - term        - Terminal-style letters

And many more fonts and control files for various character sets and languages.

--------------------

-------

32	    or from the FIGlet FTP site at ftp://ftp.figlet.org/pub/figlet/

34	3.  Where can I get more fonts for FIGlet?

1006	Very little error checking is done on font and control files.  While
1007	.B FIGlet

1009	crash, using an improperly-formatted file with
1010	.B FIGlet

1015	A tab character is converted to a blank, and vertical-tab, form-feed and
1016	carriage-return are each converted to a newline.  On many systems, tabs
1017	can be handled better by piping files through
1018	.B expand
1019	before piping through

FIGlet - Frank, Ian & Glenn's Letters
======================================

FIGlet is a program that creates large characters out of ordinary screen characters.

Example:

 _ _ _          _   _     _       
| (_) | _____  | |_| |__ (_)___   
| | | |/ / _ \ | __| '_ \| / __|  
| | |   <  __/ | |_| | | | \__ \_ 
|_|_|_|\_\___|  \__|_| |_|_|___(_)

FIGlet can create characters in many different styles and can kern and "smush" 
these characters together in various ways. FIGlet output is generally reminiscent 
of the sort of "signatures" many people like to put at the end of e-mail and 
UseNet messages.

Official FIGlet web page: http://www.figlet.org/
Contact: info@figlet.org


Usage
-----

Basic usage:
    figlet [options] [message]

If no message is provided, FIGlet reads from standard input.

Examples:
    figlet Hello, world!
    echo "Hello, world!" | figlet
    figlet -f banner "Hello"


Command Line Options
--------------------

Font and Layout:
    -f <fontfile>       Use the specified font
    -d <fontdir>        Specify directory for fonts
    -c                  Center the output
    -l                  Left-align the output (default)
    -r                  Right-align the output
    -k                  Use kerning (reduce spacing between characters)
    -W                  Full-width mode (no character smushing)
    -o                  Overlap mode
    -m <mode>           Specify layout mode

Text Direction:
    -L                  Left-to-right text (default)
    -R                  Right-to-left text

Output Control:
    -w <width>          Specify output width
    -t                  Use terminal width for output
    -p                  Paragraph mode (for multi-line input)

import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'/tmp/yourwork')
from mkfont import make_font
g=[[ "A","A"]]; sp=[[" "," "]]
def g2(c): return [[c,c]]
# A2: 6 fields only, ok baseline
# A3a: only 5 numeric fields (no comment_lines) but 1 comment line present
make_font("a3a.flf", raw_header=b"flf2a$ 2 1 10 0", comments=("c",), glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A3b: only 4 numeric fields
make_font("a3b.flf", raw_header=b"flf2a$ 2 1 10", comments=(), glyphs=[sp,g2("A")], comment_lines=0)
# A4: baseline 0
make_font("a4.flf", height=2, baseline=0, glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A5: max_length 0
make_font("a5.flf", height=2, baseline=1, max_length=0, glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A6: old_layout -1
make_font("a6.flf", height=2, baseline=1, old_layout=-1, glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A7: old_layout 15
make_font("a7.flf", height=2, baseline=1, old_layout=15, glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A8: comment_lines 0
make_font("a8.flf", height=2, baseline=1, comment_lines=0, comments=(), glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A9: comment_lines larger than actual comments (glyph lines get eaten)
make_font("a9.flf", height=2, baseline=1, comment_lines=3, comments=("c1","c2","c3"), glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A10: extra junk field after all 9
make_font("a10.flf", raw_header=b"flf2a$ 2 1 10 0 1 0 0 0 EXTRA", comments=("c",), glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A11: print_direction=1
make_font("a11.flf", height=2, baseline=1, print_direction=1, glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])
# A12: print_direction=5 (invalid)
make_font("a12.flf", height=2, baseline=1, print_direction=5, glyphs=[sp,g2("A")])

# minimal tlf: height 2, glyphs for 32..126 each "X@" / "X@@" except space=" @" / " @@"
def mkfont(path, magic, hardblank, glyph_fn, height=2, oldlayout=-1, fulllayout=0, commentlines=0, maxlen=10):

        rows = glyph_fn(c)
        assert len(rows)==height
        for i,r in enumerate(rows):

# ascii glyphs: 'a' -> "aA" rows? keep it simple: row0 = chr repeated pattern
def g_ascii(c):
    ch = chr(c) if c>32 else ' '
    return [ch, ch]

def mkfont(path, magic, hardblank, glyphmap, height=2, oldlayout=-1, fulllayout=None, maxlen=10, tags=None):
    hdr = f"{magic}{hardblank} {height} {height} {maxlen} {oldlayout} 0"
    if fulllayout is not None: hdr += f" 0 {fulllayout} 0"
    lines = [hdr]
    for c in range(32,127):
        rows = glyphmap.get(c, ['  ','  '])
        for i,r in enumerate(rows):
            end = "@@" if i==height-1 else "@"
            lines.append(r+end)
    # 7 german slots
    for c in (0xC4,0xD6,0xDC,0xE4,0xF6,0xFC,0xDF):
        rows = glyphmap.get(('german',c), ['  ','  '])
        for i,r in enumerate(rows):
            end = "@@" if i==height-1 else "@"
            lines.append(r+end)
    if tags:
        for code,rows in tags:
            lines.append(f"0x{code:X} tagged")
            for i,r in enumerate(rows):
                end = "@@" if i==height-1 else "@"
                lines.append(r+end)
    open(path,"wb").write(("\n".join(lines)+"\n").encode('latin-1'))

import zipfile, shutil, gzip
std = open('/workspace/assets/standard.flf','rb').read()
emb = open('/workspace/assets/emboss.tlf','rb').read()
# 1. single-entry zip, entry named standard.flf, archive named zstd.flf (deflate)
with zipfile.ZipFile('zstd.flf','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z: z.writestr('standard.flf', std)
# 2. stored (no compression)
with zipfile.ZipFile('zstored.flf','w',zipfile.ZIP_STORED) as z: z.writestr('standard.flf', std)
# 3. entry with different internal name
with zipfile.ZipFile('zother.flf','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z: z.writestr('whatever_name.txt', std)
# 4. multi-entry: emboss first, standard second
with zipfile.ZipFile('zmulti.flf','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
    z.writestr('emboss.tlf', emb); z.writestr('standard.flf', std)
# 5. multi-entry reversed: standard first
with zipfile.ZipFile('zmulti2.flf','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
    z.writestr('standard.flf', std); z.writestr('emboss.tlf', emb)
# 6. zip with directory entry first
with zipfile.ZipFile('zdir.flf','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z:
    z.writestr('subdir/', b''); z.writestr('subdir/standard.flf', std)
# 7. zip containing tlf, archive named .tlf
with zipfile.ZipFile('zemb.tlf','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z: z.writestr('emboss.tlf', emb)
# 8. gzip'd font renamed .flf
open('gzstd.flf','wb').write(gzip.compress(std))
# 9. plain zip named .zip
shutil.copy('zstd.flf','zstd.zip')
# 10. zip of a controlfile

with zipfile.ZipFile('z8859.flc','w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as z: z.writestr('8859-2.flc', flc)
print("created")
EOF

args.content:
# 01 — CLI: command-line parsing and informational behavior

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (FIGlet 2.2.5-like). All experiments were run with
`-d /workspace/fonts` unless noted. Scratch files lived in `/tmp/yourwork`.

Throughout this document:
- `PROG` = basename of `argv[0]` (everything after the last `/`; if no `/`, the whole string).
- `ARGV0` = `argv[0]` verbatim, exactly as invoked.

These two are used by *different* messages — see §2.

---

## 1. The `Usage:` text (exact bytes)

```
Usage: PROG [ -cklnoprstvxDELNRSWX ] [ -d fontdirectory ]
              [ -f fontfile ] [ -m smushmode ] [ -w outputwidth ]
              [ -C controlfile ] [ -I infocode ] [ message ]
```

- Continuation lines are indented with exactly **14 spaces**.
- `PROG` is the **basename** of `argv[0]`, verified via a symlink `/tmp/yourwork/myfig`
  (`Usage: myfig ...`) and via `bash -c 'exec -a "weird/path/prog" ...'` (`Usage: prog ...`).
- The text ends with a single `\n` after `[ message ]`. No trailing blank line.
- Destination stream and exit code depend on *why* it was printed:
  - Option errors (unknown option, missing argument, `-F`): **stderr**, exit **1**.
  - `-v` / `-I 0`: **stdout**, exit **0** (usage is the tail of the version text, see §6).

## 2. Program name in messages: two conventions

- **glibc getopt errors** use `ARGV0` **verbatim** (not basename) and glibc's exact wording,
  e.g. invoked as `/workspace/executable -z`:
  ```
  /workspace/executable: invalid option -- 'z'
  ```
  Via the symlink: `/tmp/yourwork/myfig: invalid option -- 'z'`.
- **The program's own messages** (`Usage:`, font/control-file errors, the `-F` text) use the
  **basename**, e.g.:
  ```
  executable: standard: Unable to open font file
  ```
  and via symlink: `myfig: standard: Unable to open font file`.

## 3. Option parsing model (glibc `getopt`)

- Short options only. No long options exist: any `--xyz` is parsed as bundled short options
  starting with `-`, producing e.g. for `--foo`:
  ```
  ARGV0: invalid option -- '-'
  Usage: ...
  ```
  on stderr, exit **1**. (`--help` and `-h` behave the same way: `invalid option -- '-'` /
  `invalid option -- 'h'`, stderr, exit 1. There is no help text.)
- **Bundling works**: `-ptk` ≡ `-p -t -k`. An argument-taking option inside a bundle consumes
  the rest of the bundle: `-pw40` ≡ `-p -w 40`; attached args also work for all of
  `-I2`, `-w40`, `-m0`, `-m-1`, `-w-7`.
- **Permutation**: options may appear after message words; getopt permutes them.
  `figlet hello -p world` renders `hello world` with `-p` applied.
  **Exception**: with `POSIXLY_CORRECT=1` in the environment, permutation is disabled —
  `figlet hi -p` then renders the literal message `hi -p`. (Vanilla glibc getopt behavior;
  the optstring has no leading `-`/`+`.)
- `--` ends option parsing and is consumed (not part of the message). A second `--` is a
  message word: `figlet -- -- x` renders `-- x`. `figlet hi --` renders just `hi`
  (md5-identical to `figlet hi`).
- A lone `-` is **not** an option; it is a message word (renders as `-`).

### Options taking arguments

`-d -f -w -m -C -I` require an argument. Missing argument (e.g. `figlet -f`) → stderr:

```
ARGV0: option requires an argument -- 'f'
Usage: ... (as above)
```

exit **1**. Same shape for `d w m C I`.

### Repeated options

Last one wins for `-d` (`-d /tmp -d /workspace/fonts -I2` → `/workspace/fonts`),
`-f` (`-f small -f standard -I3` → `standard`), and `-w` (see §5 for the `<1` exception).

## 4. Unknown options

`figlet -z` → stderr, exit **1**:

```
ARGV0: invalid option -- 'z'
Usage: PROG [ -cklnoprstvxDELNRSWX ] [ -d fontdirectory ]
              [ -f fontfile ] [ -m smushmode ] [ -w outputwidth ]
              [ -C controlfile ] [ -I infocode ] [ message ]
```

## 5. Numeric option parsing: plain `atoi()` semantics

All three numeric options (`-w`, `-m`, `-I`) are parsed with `atoi` (glibc): leading
whitespace and sign accepted, parsing stops at the first non-digit, non-numeric → `0`,
and **out-of-range values wrap/truncate to `int`** (observed: `4294967296` → 0,
`4294967297` → 1, `2147483648` → −2147483648, `999999999999999999999` → −1 via
`strtol` clamp to `LONG_MAX` then truncation). No error is ever reported for bad numbers.

### `-w outputwidth`

- Values **< 1 are silently ignored** — the previous width is kept (not an error, not a
  clamp to 80 at parse time):
  - `-w abc`, `-w 0`, `-w -5`, `-w 999999999999999999999` alone → width stays at the default `80`
    (verified byte-identical output to `-w 80`, and `-I4` prints `80`).
  - `-w 100 -w 0 -I4` → `100` (the `-w 0` was ignored, not clamped).
  - `-w 4294967296 -I4` → `80` (atoi → 0 → ignored); `-w 4294967297 -I4` → `1`.
- Effective width is order-dependent with `-t` only through normal assignment;
  see `-t` below.

### `-t` (terminal width)

- Reads the width of **stdout only** (TIOCGWINSZ on fd 1). If stdout is not a tty, nothing
  changes (stays 80 or whatever `-w` set). A tty on stderr does **not** count
  (verified: stdout=pipe, stderr=pty width 111 → `-I4` prints `80`).
- If the tty reports width 0, the `-t` is **ignored** (previous value kept), same rule as
  `-w` with `<1`: `-w 100 -t` on a width-0 pty → `100`; on a width-55 pty → `55`.
- Order matters: `-w 30 -t -I4` on a width-100 pty → `100`; `-t -w 30 -I4` → `30`.
- `COLUMNS` env var is **not** consulted.

### `-m smushmode`

- `atoi` parsed (`-m abc` → 0; `-m=-1` → 0 because atoi(`=-1`)=0; `-m 4294967296` → 0).
- Observed mapping (tested by rendering; rule-level smushing details belong to the
  smushing notes):
  - `-m 0` ≡ `-k` (kerning) — byte-identical output.
  - `-m v` for `v > 0`: overrides the font's smush mode; observations are consistent with
    an effective mode of `(v & 63) | 128`:
    `-m 15` ≡ `-m 143` ≡ `-m 191` ≡ `-m 24463` ≡ default on rule-1..4 inputs;
    `-m 64` ≡ `-m 128` (both → 128: smush with no rules); `-m 99999` (≡ 31|128) matched the
    default on the test inputs.
  - `-m -1`: a distinct mode — output is **wider than `-k`** (no kerning at all; every glyph
    at full advance width).
  - `-m v` for `v ≤ -2` (`-m -2`, `-m -3`, `-m -100`): behaves as if `-m` was never given
    (font default smushing; byte-identical to no `-m` and to `-s` on `standard.flf`).

### `-I infocode`

See §6. `atoi` parsed: `-I abc` ≡ `-I 0`; `-I 2xyz` → 2; `-I ' 1'` → 1;
`-I 4294967299` → 3; `-I 4294967296` → 0.

## 6. `-v` and `-I` informational output

### Semantics

- `-v` is exactly `-I 0` (byte-identical stdout, verified by md5).
- There is a single internal infocode variable; `-v` sets it to 0, `-I n` sets it to n.
  **Only the last `-v`/`-I` on the command line takes effect** and it is executed **once,
  after the entire command line has been parsed**. Consequences:
  - `-I 1 -I 4` prints only `80`. `-I 1 -v` prints the version text. `-v -I 1` prints `20205`.
  - Order relative to other options is irrelevant: `-I 2 -d /tmp` and `-d /tmp -I 2` both
    print `/tmp`; `-I 3 -f small` ≡ `-f small -I 3` → `small`; `-I 4 -w 120` ≡
    `-w 120 -I 4` → `120`; `-I4` after/before `-t` on a pty both give the tty width.
- If the final infocode is **≥ 0**: the info is printed to **stdout**, the message (if any)
  is **not** rendered, stdin is not read, and the program exits **0** — even for codes with
  no output (see table). No font file is loaded or needed (`-f nosuchfont -I 3` prints
  `nosuchfont`, exit 0; `-I 1..5` work with no valid font directory at all).
- If the final infocode is **negative** (`-I -1`, `-I -2`, `-I -99999`): no info is printed;
  the program proceeds **normally** (renders the message / reads stdin). This makes
  `-I -1` the way to "cancel" an earlier `-v`/`-I`.

### Output codes (each result followed by a single `\n` on stdout, exit 0)

| code | stdout | notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| `0`  | version + copyright + usage (full text below) | ≡ `-v` |
| `1`  | `20205` | version as int (2.2.5 → 20205) |
| `2`  | current font directory, verbatim | default `/usr/local/share/figlet`; value of last `-d`, else `$FIGLET_FONTDIR`, else the compiled default; trailing slash/empty preserved as given (`-d '' -I2` prints just `\n`) |
| `3`  | current font name | default `standard`; value of last `-f` with a trailing `.flf`/`.tlf` suffix stripped **case-insensitively** (`small.flf`→`small`, `foo.FLF`→`foo`, `foo.tlf`→`foo`, `a.flf.flf`→`a.flf`, `.flf`→empty, `646-de.flc`→`646-de.flc` unchanged, `./small` unchanged) |
| `4`  | current output width | default `80`; honors `-w`/`-t` final value |
| `5`  | `flf2 tlf2` | supported font formats (exact string, one space, then `\n`) |
| `≥6` | *(nothing)* | e.g. 6, 7, 100: no output, no message rendered, exit 0 |
| `<0` | *(nothing; normal rendering proceeds)* | |

### Exact `-v` / `-I 0` stdout (all of it, then exit 0)

```
FIGlet Copyright (C) 1991-2012 Glenn Chappell, Ian Chai, John Cowan,
Christiaan Keet and Claudio Matsuoka

`-F` is compiled into the optstring and handled specially. `figlet -F` (with or without
other args, e.g. `-F hi`) prints to **stderr**, exit **1**:

  - `figlet a ''` → message `a␣` → 6 rows, each 8 wide (trailing space kept!).

  trailing space on the `a` line).

  (`echo piped | figlet arg` ≡ `figlet arg`).
- No message words → read stdin until EOF:
  - Empty stdin (`</dev/null`): no output, exit **0**.
  - `echo ""` (one empty line): 6 blank rows.
  - A final line without trailing newline is still rendered: `printf 'hi'` ≡ `printf 'hi\n'`.

- Used **only when `-d` is absent**; any `-d` overrides it regardless of order
  (`FIGLET_FONTDIR=/workspace/fonts figlet -d /tmp -I2` → `/tmp`;
  `FIGLET_FONTDIR=/tmp/yourwork figlet -d /workspace/fonts -I2` → `/workspace/fonts`).

  no trailing slash is added for display; relative values are relative to the cwd.

  `\n`, and `FIGLET_FONTDIR= figlet hi` fails with `PROG: standard: Unable to open font file`

  one literal directory named `fd1:/tmp/yourwork/fd2`-style; fonts inside `fd2` are not found

  **`/usr/local/share/figlet`** (shown by `-I2`; font loading fails there on this system with

- `-f name`: the loader tries `<fontdir>/<name>.flf` (and presumably `.tlf`) **first**, then

  (`-f /workspace/fonts/small.flf -I3` → `/workspace/fonts/small`).

- Failure to open the font: stderr `PROG: <fontname-as-given>: Unable to open font file`,
  exit **1** (fontname printed exactly as passed to `-f`, e.g. `nosuch`, or `standard` when
  the default font can't be found).

| situation | exit |
|---|---|
| normal render (args or stdin), including empty stdin | 0 |
| `-v` / any `-I n` with n ≥ 0 (including codes with no output) | 0 |
| unknown option / `-h` / any `--long` | 1 |

| `-F` | 1 |
| font file cannot be opened | 1 |
| control file cannot be opened | 1 |

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (FIGlet 2.2.5-like). All experiments were run with
`-d /workspace/fonts` unless noted. Scratch files lived in `/tmp/yourwork`.

Throughout this document:
- `PROG` = basename of `argv[0]` (everything after the last `/`; if no `/`, the whole string).
- `ARGV0` = `argv[0]` verbatim, exactly as invoked.

These two are used by *different* messages — see §2.

---

## 1. The `Usage:` text (exact bytes)

```
Usage: PROG [ -cklnoprstvxDELNRSWX ] [ -d fontdirectory ]
              [ -f fontfile ] [ -m smushmode ] [ -w outputwidth ]
              [ -C controlfile ] [ -I infocode ] [ message ]
```

- Continuation lines are indented with exactly **14 spaces**.
- `PROG` is the **basename** of `argv[0]`, verified via a symlink `/tmp/yourwork/myfig`
  (`Usage: myfig ...`) and via `bash -c 'exec -a "weird/path/prog" ...'` (`Usage: prog ...`).
- The text ends with a single `\n` after `[ message ]`. No trailing blank line.
- Destination stream and exit code depend on *why* it was printed:
  - Option errors (unknown option, missing argument, `-F`): **stderr**, exit **1**.
  - `-v` / `-I 0`: **stdout**, exit **0** (usage is the tail of the version text, see §6).

## 2. Program name in messages: two conventions

- **glibc getopt errors** use `ARGV0` **verbatim** (not basename) and glibc's exact wording,
  e.g. invoked as `/workspace/executable -z`:
  ```
  /workspace/executable: invalid option -- 'z'
  ```
  Via the symlink: `/tmp/yourwork/myfig: invalid option -- 'z'`.
- **The program's own messages** (`Usage:`, font/control-file errors, the `-F` text) use the
  **basename**, e.g.:
  ```
  executable: standard: Unable to open font file
  ```
  and via symlink: `myfig: standard: Unable to open font file`.

## 3. Option parsing model (glibc `getopt`)

- Short options only. No long options exist: any `--xyz` is parsed as bundled short options
  starting with `-`, producing e.g. for `--foo`:
  ```
  ARGV0: invalid option -- '-'
  Usage: ...
  ```
  on stderr, exit **1**. (`--help` and `-h` behave the same way: `invalid option -- '-'` /
  `invalid option -- 'h'`, stderr, exit 1. There is no help text.)
- **Bundling works**: `-ptk` ≡ `-p -t -k`. An argument-taking option inside a bundle consumes
  the rest of the bundle: `-pw40` ≡ `-p -w 40`; attached args also work for all of
  `-I2`, `-w40`, `-m0`, `-m-1`, `-w-7`.
- **Permutation**: options may appear after message words; getopt permutes them.
  `figlet hello -p world` renders `hello world` with `-p` applied.
  **Exception**: with `POSIXLY_CORRECT=1` in the environment, permutation is disabled —
  `figlet hi -p` then renders the literal message `hi -p`. (Vanilla glibc getopt behavior;
  the optstring has no leading `-`/`+`.)
- `--` ends option parsing and is consumed (not part of the message). A second `--` is a
  message word: `figlet -- -- x` renders `-- x`. `figlet hi --` renders just `hi`
  (md5-identical to `figlet hi`).
- A lone `-` is **not** an option; it is a message word (renders as `-`).

### Options taking arguments

`-d -f -w -m -C -I` require an argument. Missing argument (e.g. `figlet -f`) → stderr:

```
ARGV0: option requires an argument -- 'f'
Usage: ... (as above)
```

exit **1**. Same shape for `d w m C I`.

### Repeated options

Last one wins for `-d` (`-d /tmp -d /workspace/fonts -I2` → `/workspace/fonts`),
`-f` (`-f small -f standard -I3` → `standard`), and `-w` (see §5 for the `<1` exception).

## 4. Unknown options

`figlet -z` → stderr, exit **1**:

```
ARGV0: invalid option -- 'z'
Usage: PROG [ -cklnoprstvxDELNRSWX ] [ -d fontdirectory ]
              [ -f fontfile ] [ -m smushmode ] [ -w outputwidth ]
              [ -C controlfile ] [ -I infocode ] [ message ]
```

## 5. Numeric option parsing: plain `atoi()` semantics

All three numeric options (`-w`, `-m`, `-I`) are parsed with `atoi` (glibc): leading
whitespace and sign accepted, parsing stops at the first non-digit, non-numeric → `0`,
and **out-of-range values wrap/truncate to `int`** (observed: `4294967296` → 0,
`4294967297` → 1, `2147483648` → −2147483648, `999999999999999999999` → −1 via
`strtol` clamp to `LONG_MAX` then truncation). No error is ever reported for bad numbers.

### `-w outputwidth`

- Values **< 1 are silently ignored** — the previous width is kept (not an error, not a
  clamp to 80 at parse time):
  - `-w abc`, `-w 0`, `-w -5`, `-w 999999999999999999999` alone → width stays at the default `80`

  - `-w 100 -w 0 -I4` → `100` (the `-w 0` was ignored, not clamped).
  - `-w 4294967296 -I4` → `80` (atoi → 0 → ignored); `-w 4294967297 -I4` → `1`.
- Effective width is order-dependent with `-t` only through normal assignment;
  see `-t` below.

### `-t` (terminal width)

- Reads the width of **stdout only** (TIOCGWINSZ on fd 1). If stdout is not a tty, nothing
  changes (stays 80 or whatever `-w` set). A tty on stderr does **not** count
  (verified: stdout=pipe, stderr=pty width 111 → `-I4` prints `80`).
- If the tty reports width 0, the `-t` is **ignored** (previous value kept), same rule as
  `-w` with `<1`: `-w 100 -t` on a width-0 pty → `100`; on a width-55 pty → `55`.

- `COLUMNS` env var is **not** consulted.

- `atoi` parsed (`-m abc` → 0; `-m=-1` → 0 because atoi(`=-1`)=0; `-m 4294967296` → 0).
- Observed mapping (tested by rendering; rule-level smushing details belong to the
  smushing notes):
  - `-m 0` ≡ `-k` (kerning) — byte-identical output.
  - `-m v` for `v > 0`: overrides the font's smush mode; observations are consistent with
    an effective mode of `(v & 63) | 128`:
    `-m 15` ≡ `-m 143` ≡ `-m 191` ≡ `-m 24463` ≡ default on rule-1..4 inputs;
    `-m 64` ≡ `-m 128` (both → 128: smush with no rules); `-m 99999` (≡ 31|128) matched the
    default on the test inputs.
  - `-m -1`: a distinct mode — output is **wider than `-k`** (no kerning at all; every glyph
    at full advance width).
  - `-m v` for `v ≤ -2` (`-m -2`, `-m -3`, `-m -100`): behaves as if `-m` was never given
    (font default smushing; byte-identical to no `-m` and to `-s` on `standard.flf`).

### `-I infocode`

See §6. `atoi` parsed: `-I abc` ≡ `-I 0`; `-I 2xyz` → 2; `-I ' 1'` → 1;

payload.resultSummary:
Findings written to `/workspace/notes/01-cli.md`. 10-line summary:

1. Usage text is exactly `Usage: <basename> [ -cklnoprstvxDELNRSWX ] [ -d fontdirectory ]` + two 14-space-indented continuation lines; goes to **stderr/exit 1** on option errors, but to **stdout/exit 0** as the tail of `-v`/`-I 0`.
2. Two program-name conventions: glibc getopt errors (`invalid option -- 'z'`, `option requires an argument -- 'f'`) print **argv[0] verbatim**; the program's own messages (Usage, `Unable to open font file`, `-F`) print the **basename**.
3. Parsing is vanilla glibc getopt: bundling (`-ptk`, `-pw40`), permutation of options after message words (disabled by `POSIXLY_CORRECT=1`), `--` ends options, lone `-` is a message word; no long options (`--help` → `invalid option -- '-'`, exit 1).
4. All numeric options use raw `atoi` with no errors: `-w`/`-t` values < 1 are **ignored** (keep previous width, default 80; `-w 100 -w 0` → 100); overflow wraps to int (`4294967296`→0→ignored; `4294967297`→1).
5. `-t` reads the width of **stdout only** (a tty on stderr doesn't count; `COLUMNS` ignored; tty width 0 is ignored); last of `-w`/`-t` wins by assignment order.
6. `-m`: 0 ≡ `-k`; >0 behaves as `(v & 63) | 128` (e.g. 15 ≡ 143 ≡ 24463 ≡ font default; 64 ≡ 128); **-1 is a distinct full-width mode** (wider than `-k`); ≤ −2 behaves as if `-m` was never given.
7. `-v` ≡ `-I 0`; a single infocode variable, **only the last `-v`/`-I` executes, once, after full parsing** (so `-d`/`-f`/`-w`/`-t` order never matters); codes: 1→`20205`, 2→fontdir verbatim, 3→font name with `.flf`/`.tlf` suffix stripped case-insensitively, 4→width, 5→`flf2 tlf2`, ≥6→no output; any code ≥0 suppresses the message and exits 0 without loading fonts; negative codes cancel info and render normally.
8. Message words join with one space; an **empty word is a line break**: non-last empty → `\n`, last empty → nothing (so `figlet ''` prints nothing, `'' ''` prints one blank line, `a '' b` keeps a trailing space after `a`); args present ⇒ stdin never read; unterminated final stdin line still renders.
9. `FIGLET_FONTDIR` is used verbatim **only when `-d` is absent** (any `-d` wins), an empty value is honored (not treated as unset), colon-separated paths are **not** split; default is `/usr/local/share/figlet`; font lookup tries `<fontdir>/<name>.flf` first, then the name as given (cwd fallback).
10. `-F` is special-cased: stderr, exit 1, `<basename>: illegal option -- F` (no quotes) + Usage + blank line + the exact figlist paragraph (`...available\nfrom  http://www.figlet.org/under UNIX utilities.` — note the double spaces).

# 06 — Input Charset and Stream Handling

Binary: `/workspace/executable`, reports version `20205` (FIGlet 2.2.5) via `-I1`.
All experiments run with `-d /workspace/fonts` (default font = `standard`, height 6).
Unless stated otherwise, no control file was loaded (equivalent to `-N`).

## 0. Processing pipeline (deduced order)

- `0x80–0xBF` (lone continuation): **silently dropped** (consumed, no codepoint, no output). E.g. `\xbf` renders nothing, vs `¿` in Latin-1 mode.
- `0xC0–0xDF`: reads 1 more byte.
- `0xE0–0xEF`: reads 2 more bytes.
- `0xF0–0xF7`: reads 3 more bytes.
- `0xF8–0xFB`: reads 4 more bytes (old-style 5-byte UTF-8!).
- `0xFC–0xFD`: reads 5 more bytes (6-byte).
- `0xFE–0xFF`: **silently dropped** as single bytes.

```
cp = (lead & mask_lead) | ((b1 & 0x3F) << 6*(n-1)) | ... | (bn & 0x3F)

- **Codepoints > U+10FFFF not rejected**: `\xf5...` decodes by masking (lead & 0x03? → 5-byte-style high bits), no glyph → dropped.

(§5): `\xce\xb1` (Greek α, U+03B1), `\xe4\xb8\xad` (CJK 中, U+4E2D), `\xe2\x82\xac` (€) all produce
nothing — a line containing only such chars + `\n` prints 6 empty lines.

`ESC A` under `-C utf8` renders exactly `A`. The ESC→+0x100 mechanism exists ONLY in default (Latin-1) mode.

| input char | codepoint | char |
|---|---|---|
| `[` (0x5B) | 196 (0xC4) | Ä |
| `\` (0x5C) | 214 (0xD6) | Ö |
| `]` (0x5D) | 220 (0xDC) | Ü |
| `{` (0x7B) | 228 (0xE4) | ä |
| `|` (0x7C) | 246 (0xF6) | ö |
| `}` (0x7D) | 252 (0xFC) | ü |
| `~` (0x7E) | 223 (0xDF) | ß |

`-E` disables it; later options win (`-D -E` = off; `-D` alone = on). `-D` also works in UTF-8 mode

- The char produces **zero output columns** — it is not printed as-is, not blank-padded, not '?'.

  `A<ESC>\xe9B` row 1 = `    _     ____  ` — exactly ONE extra blank column, because A and B can

- **No input buffer limit observed**: a single 10,000-char line (and 100,000-char line) processes
  fine; no truncation, no crash, exit 0.

  starts a NEW output line. Input newlines are independent of this. 100 × `A` at default width →
  13 output lines: 12 lines of 8 A's (72 columns each) + 1 line of 4 A's (36 columns).

  wider than the usable width is truncated on the right, NOT dropped. (Precise smush-fit arithmetic

  char on its own line.

- If any message args are present, **stdin is ignored entirely** (verified: `echo hi | figlet THERE`
  renders only `THERE`).
- Args are joined into one message. Determined join rule (verified against 12 arg combinations):
  iterate args left to right; between consecutive args insert a separator which is
  **`" "` (space) if the left-hand arg is non-empty, `"\n"` (newline) if the left-hand arg is empty**.
  Nothing is appended after the last arg. Verified equivalences (arg form == stdin string):
  - `A B` == `A B`; `A B C` == `A B C`
  - `A '' B` == `A \nB` (empty arg → newline; the space before it from the previous separator remains)
  - `'' A` == `\nA`; `A ''` == `A \n` (renders as `A ` line only); `'' ''` == `\n`;
    `'' '' ''` == `\n\n`; `A '' '' B` == `A \n\nB`; `''` alone == empty (no output at all)
- Embedded `\n` inside a single arg (`$'A\nB'`) acts as a line break, exactly like stdin.
- `--` ends option processing: `figlet -- -f` renders the literal text `-f`, exit 0.
- Unknown option: stderr `executable: invalid option -- 'z'` followed by a 3-line Usage text, **exit 1**.
- Note: options may follow message args (getopt permutation): `figlet A -k B` renders `A B` with -k in effect.
- Exit codes observed: normal rendering (even all-dropped/empty input) = **0**;
  missing font file: stderr `<progname>: <path>: Unable to open font file`, exit **1**;
  missing control file: `... Unable to open control file`, exit **1**.

| Input | Default mode | `-C utf8` mode |
|---|---|---|
| byte 0xE9 | é (U+00E9) | 2-byte lead; consumes next byte, masks it in |
| 0xC3 0xA9 | `Ã` + `©` | é |
| 0xC3 EOF | Ã (U+00C3) | ÿ (U+00FF, EOF masks as 0x3F) |
| 0xC0 0xAF | À + ¯ | `/` (overlong accepted) |
| 0x80–0x9F | dropped | dropped (lone continuation) |
| 0xA0 | space glyph | 2-byte-lead? no — 0xA0 is 0b10100000 → lone continuation → **dropped** |
| TAB / CR / LF / VT / FF | space / break / break / break / break | same |
| NUL, 0x01–0x08, 0x0E–0x1A, 0x1C–0x1F, 0x7F | dropped | dropped |
| ESC (0x1B) | prefix: next byte + 0x100 | dropped (ordinary codepoint 0x1B) |
| 0xFE, 0xFF | þ , ÿ glyphs | dropped |
| 0xF8–0xFD | ø–ý glyphs | 5/6-byte leads, consume 4/5 more bytes |
| char with no glyph | dropped, blocks smush (1-col gap effect) | same |

(Note the asymmetry: 0xA0 renders as space in default mode but is swallowed as a stray
continuation byte in UTF-8 mode.)
